text: Lesson 12 ended with a single service and a default domain. Two more pieces usually sit in front of that before real traffic reaches it, and they're not the same job.

A load balancer spreads traffic across multiple instances of the same service, so one crashed instance doesn't take the whole app down. An API gateway handles routing, auth, and rate limiting before a request ever reaches your application code.

A real gateway console flow starts with creating a resource. The proxy resource pattern, slash proxy plus, is common for AI apps -- one resource forwards everything under a path to your backend's own internal routing.

Once a resource is wired to a backend, you deploy it to a stage and get a real invoke URL, distinct from your service's own address. That same stage screen is where rate and burst limits live, enforced at the gateway.
You can even test a method directly in the console -- a real request routed through the gateway, with no separate HTTP client needed yet.
This matters more for an AI app than a plain CRUD API. Prompt payloads are large, inference calls are slow and expensive, and a careless client loop can hammer a model endpoint fast.
Gateway-level rate limits catch that before it becomes an autoscaling bill or an outage. Next up: shipping a new version of that service without taking it down -- blue-green deployment.
